LabourMarketFramework – User Guide

A Python toolkit for US labour-market and further-education analysis

Authors

Allotey Kelvin, Lloyd

Braun, Finn

Bruehwiler, Nils

Troillet, Cyril

Published

May 20, 2026

0 Overview

LabourMarketFramework is a Python class for analysing US labour-market conditions and the relationship to further education since 2000. The class runs through a local DuckDB database with three functionality layers: data access, helpers, and output methods. There are five output methods that produce figures and tables visible in the analysis brief.

Topic and research question:

Do young Americans pursue further education in response to deteriorating labour market conditions in the United States since 2000?

The class is database-agnostic. You can swap the DuckDB file to analyze other countries, recessions or sectors. The methods will work the same without having to adjust code.

1 Getting started

1. 1 Requirements

  • Python 3.13 or later
  • uv (Python environment and dependency manager)
  • A free FRED API key

1.2 Install

From the repository root:

uv sync

This creates .venv/ and installs every runtime dependency

(duckdb, pandas, matplotlib, fredapi, python-dotenv, ipykernel, jupyter).

1.3 FRED API key

data/build_fred.py reads your key from a .env file at the repository root. A template .env.example is in the repo. Create your own .env:

FRED_API_KEY=your_actual_key_here

.env is in .gitignore so your key stays local and protected.

1.4 Build the database (one time process)

uv run python data/build_fred.py

From the repository root run the script below. The script fetches the selected series from the FRED, joins the master’s enrollment table, and creates data/fred.db (the database). The committed fred.db already contains everything. This step is only necessary if you want to start from scratch.

Once this step is completed the class reads only from the database. No notebook ever calls the FRED API or reads a CSV.

1.5 First call

import sys
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path("..") / "src"))
from labour_market_framework import LabourMarketFramework

lmf = LabourMarketFramework(db_path=Path("..") / "data" / "fred.db")

lmf is the class instance you call methods on. The constructor opens a read only connection to the database and caches the list of available series IDs, so subsequent input validation is fast.

2. How the class is organised

The class has three layers, grouped under section comments in src/labour_market_framework.py:

  1. Data access - These read from the DuckDB database (chap. 3.2)

    • available_series, load_series, load_category.

  2. Helpers - They clean, transform and reshape series so output methods can stay focused (chap. 3.3)

    • align_frequencies, tag_recession_episodes, plus internal validators and the recession-shading and z-score utilities.

  3. Output methods - These produce the figures, tables and computed metrics (chap. 4)

    1. plot_beveridge_curve

    2. descriptive_stats

    3. compute_stress_index

    4. plot_enrollment_overlay

    5. plot_stress_index_vs_enrollment

    Most users only ever call output methods directly. The data access and helper methods are exposed for cases where you want to query the database yourself or build a custom view.

3. Method reference

Every public method on the class is listed here with its signature, purpose, arguments, return value and the exceptions it raises. Examples for the output methods follow in the next section.

3.1 Constructor and lifecycle

[1] LabourMarketFramework(db_path="data/fred.db")

  • Open a read only DuckDB connection at db_path and cache the list of available series IDs for fast validation later.

Arguments

  • db_path : str | pathlib.Path, default "data/fred.db". Path to the DuckDB database.

Returns

  • The class instance.

Raises

  • FileNotFoundError if the database file does not exist. Error message hints at running data/build_fred.py.

[2] close()

  • Close the underlying DuckDB connection.

Arguments/Return/Raises: none.

3.2 Data access

[3] available_series(category=None)

  • Return metadata for every series in the database, or filter to one category.

Arguments

  • category : str | None, default None. If given, restricts the result to series with this category. Valid categories: 'beveridge', 'stress_index', 'recession', 'education', 'enrollment'.

Returns

  • pandas.DataFrame with columns series_id, title, units, frequency, seasonal_adjustment, category.

Raises

  • ValueError if the category is not present in the database (error message lists the valid options).

[4] load_series(series_id, start_date=None, end_date=None)

  • Read one time series from the database, optionally clipped by date.

Arguments

  • series_id : str. Must exist in the database.
  • start_date : str | None, default None. Inclusive lower bound, 'YYYY-MM-DD'.
  • end_date : str | None, default None. Inclusive upper bound, 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

Returns

  • pandas.Series named after series_id, indexed by DatetimeIndex.

Raises

  • TypeError if series_id or dates are not strings; ValueError if series_id is unknown or dates are malformed or inverted. start_date must be strictly before end_date.

[5] load_category(category, start_date=None, end_date=None)

  • Load every series in a category at once.

Arguments

  • category : str. One of the valid categories above.
  • start_date, end_date : str | None, default None. Same as load_series.

Returns

  • dict[str, pandas.Series] keyed by series_id.

Raises

  • propagated from available_series and load_series.

3.3 Helpers

[6] align_frequencies(series_dict, freq="MS", how="inner")

  • Resample multiple series to a common frequency and join them into one DataFrame.

Arguments

  • series_dict : dict[str, pandas.Series].
  • freq : str, default "MS". Any pandas offset alias works ("MS" = month start, "YS" = year start, etc.).
  • how : str, default "inner". Must be "inner" or "outer".

Returns

  • pandas.DataFrame with one column per series.

Raises

  • ValueError if series_dict is empty, if how is not "inner" or "outer", or if an annual series is inner-joined at a monthly freq. The last case is caught explicitly because the inner join would silently drop almost all rows. To align annual data with monthly data, pass freq="YS" (downsample to annual means) or how="outer" (keep the upsampled NaN months visible).

[7] tag_recession_episodes(start_date=None, end_date=None)

  • Identify continuous NBER recession periods from the USREC series.

  • Useful if you want the recession dates as data (for example, to shade your own plot).

Arguments

  • start_date, end_date : str | None, default None. Restrict the scan window.

Returns

  • list[tuple[pandas.Timestamp, pandas.Timestamp]], one tuple per episode in chronological order.

Raises

  • Propagated from load_series and _validate_dates.

3.4 Internal helpers

Three private helpers exist on the class but should not be called directly:

[8] _validate_series_id: Checks that a series ID exists in the DB

[9] _validate_dates: Internal check that date strings parse and are ordered

[10] _shade_recessions: Draw grey vertical bands for each recession episode

They support the input-validation, recession-shading.

[11] _zscore: Standardises a series to mean 0 and sd 1

z-scoring is used by the public methods.

4. Output methods and examples

Every example below uses the lmf instance from the First call section above. The examples are independent: skip directly to the method you care about.

Output 1: Beveridge curve

[12] plot_beveridge_curve

Plot the Beveridge curve, the job openings rate (JTSJOR) against the unemployment rate (UNRATE). Points are coloured by year, recession months can be ringed in red.

Signature:

plot_beveridge_curve(
    start_date=None,
    end_date=None,
    annotate_recessions=True,
    cmap="plasma",
)

Arguments

  • start_date, end_date : str | None, default None. Date window.
  • annotate_recessions : bool, default True. Ring recession months in red.
  • cmap : str, default "plasma". Any matplotlib colormap name.

Returns

  • matplotlib.figure.Figure.

Raises

  • ValueError on bad dates or empty window (JOLTS data starts December 2000).

Default call:

fig = lmf.plot_beveridge_curve()

Variant:

(restricted window, no recession rings, different colormap)

fig = lmf.plot_beveridge_curve(
    start_date="2007-01-01",
    end_date="2012-12-31",
    annotate_recessions=False,
    cmap="viridis",
)

Output 2: Descriptive statistics

[13] descriptive_stats

Summary table for every series (count, mean, standard deviation, min, max), with an optional correlation matrix.

Signature:

descriptive_stats(
    series_ids=None,
    start_date=None,
    end_date=None,
    include_correlations=False,
)

Arguments

  • series_ids : list[str] | None, default None (every series).
  • start_date, end_date : str | None, default None.
  • include_correlations : bool, default False. If True, also returns the correlation matrix. The matrix covers only the monthly series and is 8x8; the annual MASTERS_ENROLLMENT is dropped to avoid mixing frequencies.

Returns

  • pandas.DataFrame (stats only), or (stats, corr) tuple when include_correlations=True.

Raises

  • ValueError on unknown series_ids or bad dates.

Default call:

lmf.descriptive_stats()

Output 3: Composite stress index

[14] compute_stress_index

Aggregate labour-market stress index: a z-scored composite of several FRED series. Higher index-values translate to worse conditions.

Signature:

compute_stress_index(
    series_ids=None,
    weights=None,
    start_date=None,
    end_date=None,
    freq="MS",
)

Arguments

  • series_ids : list[str] | None, default None (every series with category == 'stress_index').
  • weights : dict[str, float] | None, default None. Map each series id to a weight. If omitted, the class applies its default signs: UNRATE, LNS12032194, LNS14027662 get +1; JTSJOR, JTSHIL, JTSQUR, PAYEMS get -1.
  • start_date, end_date : str | None, default None.
  • freq : str, default "MS". Target frequency for the internal align_frequencies call.

Returns

  • pandas.Series named "stress_index".

Raises

  • ValueError if weights is None and any requested series_id lacks a default sign; if the keys of weights do not match series_ids, if the sum of absolute weights is zero, or if dates are invalid.

Default call:

(the project’s standard index)

stress = lmf.compute_stress_index()
print(f"Length: {len(stress)} monthly observations")
print(f"Range:  {stress.index.min().date()} to {stress.index.max().date()}")
print(f"Mean:   {stress.mean():.3f}")
print(f"Stdev:  {stress.std():.3f}")
print(stress.tail())
Length: 304 monthly observations
Range:  2000-12-01 to 2026-03-01
Mean:   0.001
Stdev:  0.859
date

2025-12-01   -0.543070
2026-01-01   -0.641413
2026-02-01   -0.470923
2026-03-01   -0.771569
Freq: MS, Name: stress_index, dtype: float64

Variant:

(Custom basket and explicit weights - two series, equal weighting)

custom = lmf.compute_stress_index(
    series_ids=["UNRATE", "JTSJOR"],
    weights={"UNRATE": +1.0, "JTSJOR": -1.0},
)
print(custom.tail())

Output 4: Enrollment overlay

[15] plot_enrollment_overlay

Overlay one FRED series and the YoY growth (%) of master’s enrollment on twin y-axes, with NBER recession bands shaded.

Signature:

plot_enrollment_overlay(
    series_id="UNRATE",
    start_date=None,
    end_date=None,
)

Arguments

  • series_id : str, default "UNRATE". The FRED series on the left axis.
  • start_date, end_date : str | None, default None.

Returns

  • matplotlib.figure.Figure.

Raises

  • ValueError if series_id is unknown, dates are invalid, or the window contains no data for one of the two series.

Default call:

(UNRATE versus enrollment growth)

fig = lmf.plot_enrollment_overlay()

Variant:

(different FRED series on the left axis)

fig = lmf.plot_enrollment_overlay(series_id="JTSJOR")

Output 5: Stress index versus enrollment

[16] plot_stress_index_vs_enrollment

The broader companion to plot_enrollment_overlay. The left axis is the full composite stress index instead of a single FRED series.

Signature:

plot_stress_index_vs_enrollment(
    start_date=None,
    end_date=None,
    enrollment_metric="growth",
)

Arguments

  • start_date, end_date : str | None, default None.
  • enrollment_metric : str, default "growth". Same values as plot_enrollment_overlay.
  • This mechanism allows for the development of the class (e.g. future inclusion of metric: log growth)

Returns

  • matplotlib.figure.Figure.

Raises

  • ValueError on bad dates, empty window, or unsupported enrollment_metric.

Default call:

(growth view of enrollment)

fig = lmf.plot_stress_index_vs_enrollment()

Variant:

(level view of enrollment)

fig = lmf.plot_stress_index_vs_enrollment(enrollment_metric="level")

5. Series catalogue

The committed database contains nine series, grouped into five categories. The category is what available_series(category=...) and load_category(category=...) filter on.

Category Series IDs
beveridge JTSJOR, UNRATE
stress_index JTSQUR, JTSHIL, LNS12032194, PAYEMS
recession USREC
education LNS14027662
enrollment MASTERS_ENROLLMENT

6. Errors you might see

Each method validates its inputs before doing any work and raises with a message that explains what went wrong and how to fix it. Four common cases:

  • FileNotFoundError at instantiation: the database is not where db_path points. Run uv run python data/build_fred.py from the repo root to (re)build it.
  • ValueError: Series 'X' not in database. Available: [...]: you passed a series_id that does not exist. The error lists every valid ID.
  • ValueError: start_date 'X' is not a valid date. Expected format: YYYY-MM-DD.: a date argument is malformed. Use the 'YYYY-MM-DD' format.
  • ValueError: enrollment_metric must be 'growth' or 'level', got 'X'. (or similar for how in align_frequencies): a string argument is outside the allowed set. The error lists the allowed values.
